name: Movement & Physical Confidence
what: Moving because the body is yours, and finding out what it can do.
levels: Joins in movement when an adult starts it and stays alongside them.
Tries an unfamiliar physical activity when invited, with a trusted adult nearby.
Says whether an activity felt good or hard, when asked.
Takes the movement break when reminded, and takes part rather than waiting it out.
Names something their body can do now that it could not do before.
Says afterwards that they felt different once they had moved.
Chooses to move on an ordinary day without anyone suggesting it.
Gives their own reason for moving, stated as what it does for them (e.g., "I think more clearly afterwards", "I get restless if I sit all morning").
Notices during the work itself that they need to move, and goes.
Keeps moving through a stretch when the usual activity was not available, unprompted, and can explain what they put in its place and why.
Adjusts what they do when their body responds differently from how they expected, rather than stopping.
Stays with an activity they are not immediately good at, past the point where it stops being flattering.
Separates a day when rest is the right call from a day when reluctance is, and says which one it is.
Sustains a movement practice across seasons, including long stretches with nothing to train for and nobody watching.
Changes the practice on the evidence of their own record rather than on advice or fashion.
Describes moving as part of how they live rather than as a thing they do.
Sets up movement that people at very different starting points can join without embarrassment.
Notices who is being left out of physical activity, and changes the activity rather than the person.
Passes on a practice in a form someone else can actually take up and keep.

name: Fuel & Nourishment
what: Eating in a way that holds the day up.
levels: Eats with the group when an adult sets the routine.
Tries an unfamiliar food when someone they trust is eating it too.
Says when they are hungry, when asked.
Eats at the points the day is built around, on a reminder.
Names a food that helps them and one that leaves them flat.
Says afterwards that missing a meal changed how the afternoon went.
Eats before a demanding block without being told to.
Gives their own reason for what they eat, stated as how it leaves them (e.g., "I get short with people if I skip lunch").
Notices hunger while working and deals with it, rather than pushing through and paying for it later.
Keeps eating well through a disrupted stretch — a trip, an exam week, a changed timetable — unprompted, and can explain what they planned differently.
Puts together something workable from what is actually available, rather than abandoning the plan because the usual option is gone.
Recognises when they are eating out of habit or pressure rather than hunger, and names it.
Holds their own eating routine when the people around them are not holding theirs.
Sustains a way of eating across months, including stretches when it is inconvenient and nobody would notice if they stopped.
Adjusts what they eat on the evidence of how they have actually felt and worked, not on what is being promoted.
Prepares food for themselves as a matter of course rather than as an occasion.
Feeds other people, and makes it something they can join rather than receive.
Notices when someone in the group has not eaten, and acts without turning it into a remark about them.
Passes on something practical — a way of preparing, a way of planning ahead — that someone else can use.

name: Sleep & Recovery
what: Treating rest as something you do, not something that happens to you.
levels: Follows a wind-down routine an adult sets.
Says whether they slept well, when asked.
Takes a rest when an adult offers one.
Goes to bed at a set time on a reminder.
Names one thing that makes their own sleep worse.
Connects a bad night to how the following day went, once the day is over.
Protects their own bedtime on an ordinary night without being told.
Gives their own reason for it, stated in terms of the next day (e.g., "I can't hold an argument together if I've been up late").
Notices in the evening that they are heading for a short night, and changes course while there is still time.
Rebuilds a sleep routine after a stretch that broke it — travel, illness, a run of late finishes — unprompted, and can explain what they changed to get it back.
Keeps their timing roughly steady across the whole week rather than running short and repaying at the weekend.
Chooses sleep over something they genuinely wanted to do, and can say what the trade was.
Tells a single bad night apart from a pattern, and responds to each of them differently.
Holds a sleep pattern across a long stretch, including periods with no deadline pressing on it.
Adjusts the routine on the evidence of their own record rather than on general advice.
Treats recovery as part of the plan for demanding work, not as whatever is left over at the end.
Plans shared work and group time so that other people's sleep is not the thing that pays for it.
Says out loud when a group is running on too little sleep, and proposes something workable instead.
Passes on a wind-down practice in a form someone else can take up.

name: Body Signals & Self-Care
what: Reading what the body is telling you, and doing something about it.
levels: Tells an adult when something hurts or feels wrong.
Accepts help with a minor injury or illness.
Follows a care instruction an adult gives them.
Reports a symptom or an injury without waiting to be asked about it.
Deals with a small thing themselves on a reminder — water, warmth, a plaster, getting out of the sun.
Names one signal their body gives them before they are unwell or overloaded.
Acts on a body signal at the time it arrives, without being told to.
Gives their own reason for a care habit, stated as what it prevents or allows (e.g., "I stretch because otherwise my back stops me sitting through the afternoon").
Asks a question about their own health rather than waiting to be told things.
Keeps looking after themselves through a stretch when it was harder to, unprompted, and can explain what they did differently.
Checks a health claim against a second source before acting on it themselves, rather than acting on the first thing they read.
Follows through on something that takes time — a course of care, a recovery, a check-up — rather than stopping when it stops hurting.
Says what they need to an adult who is not their guide, at the point they need it.
Maintains care routines across long stretches when nothing is wrong and nothing prompts them.
Refines what they do on the evidence of what has actually worked for them, and can say what the evidence was.
Holds a limit under real pressure to exceed it, and can say why the limit is there.
Notices when someone else is pushing through something they should not be, and says so.
Makes it ordinary in a group to say that something hurts, rather than admirable to hide it.
Passes on a care practice in a form someone else can use.

name: Load & Demand
what: Knowing how much is on you, and doing something about the amount.
levels: Says when something feels like too much, when asked directly.
Lets an adult take something off them.
Works through a task an adult has broken into parts.
Says they are overloaded on a reminder, before it shows up in the work.
Lists what is currently on them when asked to.
Recognises afterwards that they took on more than fitted.
Says no, or asks for a change, before agreeing to something that will not fit — without being prompted.
Gives their own reason for managing what they carry, stated as what happens to them otherwise (e.g., "I start dropping things nobody knows I'm holding").
Notices load building while it is building, rather than after the work has already slipped.
Reshapes their commitments during a stretch heavier than any they had faced before, unprompted, and can explain what they dropped and why that one.
Chooses deliberately which thing to do less well, rather than doing everything less well by default.
Puts something down before it collapses rather than after it has.
Tells a heavy period that will end apart from a load that has quietly become permanent, and treats the two differently.
Keeps what they carry workable across a long stretch, including periods when agreeing would be much easier than declining.
Sets the shape of their commitments in advance rather than reacting to whatever arrives.
Adjusts on the evidence of their own record of what they can actually carry, not on what they wish they could.
Notices when a group has taken on more than it can hold, and says so while there is still time.
Distributes work in a way that accounts for what people are already carrying elsewhere.
Makes declining something ordinary in a group rather than a thing that has to be justified.

name: Restoration & Recovery
what: Knowing what actually restores you, and taking it.
levels: Takes a break when an adult sends them for one, and comes back.
Says whether something helped them feel better, when asked.
Uses a restoring activity an adult has set up for them.
Takes a break on a reminder, before the work has degraded.
Names one thing that restores them and one that only looks as though it does.
Recognises afterwards that they went too long without stopping.
Takes restoration on an ordinary day without being told to.
Gives their own reason for it, stated as what it gives back to them (e.g., "twenty minutes outside and I can actually read again").
Notices depletion as it arrives and responds, rather than pushing through to the end of the day and paying for it.
Finds a way to restore themselves during a period when their usual way was unavailable, unprompted, and can explain what they substituted and why.
Chooses recovery that fits what has actually depleted them, rather than applying the same remedy to everything.
Protects recovery time at a point when there was a real reason to give it up.
Tells rest that restores apart from rest that only postpones, and can say which one they just took.
Builds recovery into a long project from the start, rather than bolting it on after the depletion.
Sustains restoring practices across months, including stretches when nothing is demanding them.
Refines what they do on their own record of what has actually worked, and can say what the evidence was.
Builds recovery into shared work so it is not left to each person to solve alone.
Notices when someone else is depleted, and adjusts what is asked of them.
Makes stopping legitimate in a group rather than something that has to be earned.

name: Help-Seeking & Support
what: Asking — early enough, and from the right person.
levels: Tells an adult something is wrong when they are asked directly.
Accepts help when it is offered.
Names one adult in the school they would go to.
Asks for help on a reminder, or when the routine makes a space for it.
Says what kind of help they need, not only that they need some.
Recognises afterwards that they left it too late to ask.
Asks unprompted, at a point where the help can still change the outcome.
Gives their own reason for asking, stated as what it does for them (e.g., "I lose a week if I try to work it out alone").
Knows which person to go to for which kind of thing, and can say why that person.
Asks for help in a situation they had not faced before, unprompted, and can explain who they chose and why.
Asks again, or somewhere else, when the first attempt did not get them anywhere.
Asks for something they find embarrassing to ask for.
Tells what they can work through alone apart from what genuinely needs another person, and acts on the difference.
Keeps up the relationships they can draw on before they need them, rather than building them in a crisis.
Asks consistently across a long period, including stretches when managing alone would be less exposing.
Refines who they go to on the evidence of what has actually helped.
Is someone others come to, and knows the limits of what they can hold.
Passes a person on to the right help rather than trying to be all of it themselves.
Makes asking ordinary in a group by doing it visibly.

name: Emotion Knowledge & Vocabulary
what: Knowing what you are feeling, precisely enough to do something with it.
levels: Names a feeling as good or bad, with an adult helping them find the word.
Points to where in the body a feeling shows up, when asked.
Takes an adult's suggestion about what they might be feeling, and checks it against themselves.
Names feelings more precisely than good or bad on a reminder (e.g., frustrated, nervous, disappointed, relieved).
Says afterwards what set a feeling off.
Recognises the same feeling turning up in more than one kind of situation.
Names a feeling while it is happening, without being asked to.
Gives their own account of what the feeling is telling them, stated as what it does for them (e.g., "when I get snappy it usually means I haven't eaten").
Distinguishes two feelings that sit close together — nervous and excited, angry and hurt, tired and flat.
Reads a feeling accurately in a situation they had not been in before, unprompted, and can explain how they worked out what it was.
Holds two feelings at once and names both, rather than collapsing them into whichever is louder.
Separates the feeling itself from the story they are telling themselves about why it is there.
Recognises a feeling that has arrived from somewhere else and landed in the wrong place.
Tracks their own emotional patterns across a long stretch and describes them accurately rather than flatteringly.
Refines their own vocabulary and working model on the evidence of what has turned out to be true.
Reads their feelings as information about a situation, not as verdicts about themselves.
Helps someone else find the word for what they are feeling without supplying it for them.
Makes precise emotional language ordinary in a group rather than awkward.
Reads a group's state and names it in a form the group can actually use.

name: Coping & Recovery from Setback
what: Getting back up — and getting back up faster than last time.
levels: Accepts comfort from an adult after something has gone wrong.
Says what happened, with an adult alongside them.
Comes back to the group when an adult brings them back.
Uses a settling strategy on a reminder after a setback.
Names what went wrong, and not only who is to blame for it.
Recognises afterwards that the feeling passed.
Settles themselves after a setback without being told how.
Gives their own reason for the strategy they used, stated as what it does for them (e.g., "walking it off stops me saying something I'll have to undo").
Comes back to the thing, or the person, within a timeframe they set for themselves.
Recovers from a setback larger or more public than any they had faced before, unprompted, and can explain what they did and why that was the right thing for this one.
Chooses a different approach for a different kind of setback rather than applying the same one to all of them.
Keeps something in proportion while the feeling is insisting it is bigger than it is.
Names what they actually lost, honestly, rather than reframing it out of existence.
Recovers from repeated setbacks across a long period without the recoveries getting slower.
Refines how they recover on the evidence of what has actually worked for them before.
Takes on things carrying a real chance of failure, knowing in advance what the recovery will cost them.
Stays steady enough after a shared setback that other people can recover around them.
Talks about their own setbacks in a way that makes other people's survivable.
Notices someone stuck after a setback and offers something specific rather than sympathy.

name: Self-Regard & Self-Compassion
what: How you talk to yourself when it has gone wrong.
levels: Takes an adult's reassurance after a mistake and can settle on it.
Says one thing they did well, when asked.
Lets an adult separate the mistake from them.
Says something accurate about their own work on a reminder, rather than only harsh or only glowing.
Names a mistake as a thing that happened rather than a thing they are.
Recognises afterwards that they were harder on themselves than the situation warranted.
Speaks about their own mistake, unprompted, in terms of what happened rather than what it proves about them.
Gives their own reason for treating themselves reasonably, stated as what it does for them (e.g., "if I tear into myself I don't start again for a week").
Notices harsh self-talk while it is happening, not only afterwards.
Holds a fair view of themselves through a failure more exposed than any they had faced, unprompted, and can explain what they told themselves and why.
Takes real responsibility for something without turning it into a verdict on their worth.
Recognises that the difficulty is not unique to them, and says so without using it to avoid the responsibility.
Receives a genuine compliment and a genuine criticism with the same steadiness.
Maintains a fair and accurate view of themselves across a long stretch, including periods with little external validation.
Adjusts how they talk to themselves on the evidence of what actually gets them working again.
Holds a high standard for the work without attaching it to their standing as a person.
Speaks about their own limits in a way that makes other people's admissible.
Interrupts harsh self-talk in someone else without dismissing what they are feeling.
Sets a tone in a group where mistakes are stated plainly rather than hidden or performed.

name: Connecting & Including
what: Finding your place, and making room in it.
levels: Joins a group when an adult brings them into it.
Says who they spent the day with, when asked.
Greets someone new when an adult makes the introduction.
Joins something on a reminder rather than waiting to be brought in.
Notices that someone has been left out, once it is pointed out to them.
Says afterwards which parts of the day they felt part of.
Joins or starts something without anyone bringing them into it.
Gives their own reason for connecting, stated as what it does for them (e.g., "I go under if I spend a whole week not really talking to anyone").
Reads in the moment that someone is on the edge of a group, and makes room.
Builds a connection in a setting where they knew nobody, unprompted, and can explain how they went about it.
Reads a person whose signals are unfamiliar to them and adjusts, rather than concluding the person is unfriendly.
Includes someone whose inclusion costs them something socially.
Stays connected through a stretch when withdrawing would have been easier.
Keeps connections going across a long stretch, including with people they rarely see.
Refines how they connect on the evidence of what has actually worked, not on what is expected of them.
Belongs to more than one group, and is not diminished by moving between them.
Builds groups other people can enter, and notices who still cannot.
Changes the shape of an activity so that the person left out does not have to change themselves.
Opens a way in for someone who could not open it alone — introduces them, vouches for them, makes the space.

name: Trust & Friendship
what: Having people you can rely on, and being one of them.
levels: Names someone they would sit with, and someone they would tell if something went wrong.
Keeps a promise an adult helped them make.
Accepts help from a peer when it is offered.
Does what they said they would for someone else, on a reminder.
Names one thing that makes a friendship work.
Recognises afterwards that they let someone down.
Keeps their word to a friend with nobody tracking whether they did.
Gives their own reason for tending a friendship, stated as what it does for them (e.g., "Bat is the only person who tells me when I'm wrong").
Notices in the moment that a friend needs something, and does it then rather than later.
Keeps a friendship going through a stretch that tested it — distance, a change, competing loyalties — unprompted, and can explain what they did to hold it.
Tells a friend something true that the friend did not want to hear.
Keeps a confidence they were entrusted with, and knows the one kind of thing they must never keep.
Recognises a relationship that is taking more than it gives, and says so rather than absorbing it.
Sustains friendships across years, including periods when they were the one doing the work.
Chooses who to build with on the evidence of who has actually turned up, rather than on who is nearest.
Is relied on by people who have other options.
Connects other people to each other, and then steps back out of it.
Makes a group somewhere trust is ordinary rather than something earned by performance.
Holds a confidence, a promise or a difficult truth on behalf of a group.

name: Repair After Rupture
what: Putting a relationship back, not just ending the argument.
levels: Says sorry once an adult has helped them work out what it is for.
Stays in a repair conversation an adult is running.
Goes back to the person afterwards, with an adult alongside.
Apologises on a reminder, naming the specific thing rather than apologising in general.
Says afterwards what their own part in it was.
Accepts someone else's apology without holding it over them later.
Starts the repair themselves, with no adult setting it up.
Gives their own reason for repairing, stated in terms of the relationship rather than the rule (e.g., "I'd rather have him back than be right").
Names their own part in it at the time, not only once they have cooled down.
Repairs a rupture more serious than any they had caused or suffered before, unprompted, and can explain what they did and why they went about it that way.
Repairs with someone who did not apologise back.
Changes the behaviour that caused it, not only the feeling about it.
Recognises a rupture that cannot be repaired, and ends it without wreckage.
Keeps relationships intact across years that included real ruptures.
Repairs early, before a rupture has hardened into a pattern between them.
Adjusts how they repair on the evidence of what has actually worked with that particular person.
Helps two other people repair without taking sides and without taking over.
Makes repair ordinary in a group rather than exceptional.
Repairs something on behalf of a group they belong to.

name: Care & Contribution
what: Noticing what someone needs, and doing something about it.
levels: Helps someone when an adult asks them to.
Notices that someone is upset, once it is pointed out.
Takes part in something the group is doing for someone else.
Offers help on a reminder, before the person has had to ask.
Names what someone else might be feeling in a specific situation.
Says afterwards what difference their help actually made.
Notices someone needs something and acts on it, without being prompted.
Gives their own reason for contributing, stated in terms of the person or the place rather than the credit (e.g., "the room's better when someone's set it up and nobody ever does").
Does something for the group that nobody would have noticed if it had not been done.
Contributes to something outside their own circle, unprompted, and can explain why they chose that and what they expected it to change.
Helps in the way the person actually needs rather than the way that would feel good to give.
Keeps contributing when there is no recognition attached to it.
Recognises when helping would take something away from the person, and holds back.
Sustains a contribution across a long period, including stretches when nothing came back.
Refines what they do on the evidence of what has actually helped, rather than on what felt generous.
Holds a limit on what they give, so that the giving can last.
Builds something that goes on helping after they stop running it.
Brings other people into contributing rather than doing it all for them.
Notices a need in the wider community that nobody has named, and names it.
